title: The lake that became Kashmir
hook: before the valley there was a lake, and in the lake a demon who could not be caught while he stayed in the water
carry: the earth is holy; we ask her pardon
tomorrow: a poet sets out to tell of kings. what's the first rule he sets?

segments.voice: Yesterday, even a bow to the spire is darshan: the Varkari road ended at Pandharpur, and the walkers went home.

Before there was a valley, the old book says, there was a lake. Mountains all around, and water filling the space between them, still and deep. And in that water lived a demon. As long as he stayed in the lake, nobody could touch him; he came out to raid the lands nearby and slipped back under the surface. The gods couldn't reach him. So how do you defeat someone who hides in the water? You take away the water, and what's left is the ground a whole people will call holy.
screen: `A LAKE BETWEEN MOUNTAINS.` → `A DEMON HIDING IN THE WATER.` → `TAKE AWAY THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The book is the Nilamata Purana, a Sanskrit text of Kashmir, and here it is in paraphrase. The lake was called Satisar, the lake of Sati, the goddess. The demon in it was Jalodbhava. He couldn't be killed in his element, so the sage Kashyapa went to the gods and asked for help. Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma came. The mountain wall was opened, the water drained away, and the demon, left on dry ground, was struck down. What was left behind was a green valley, and people came to live in it. Tradition links Kashmir's name with Kashyapa, the sage who asked. Now the teaching. For Kashmiri Hindus, the valley isn't just land. Its floor was once the goddess's lake, and the rivers and springs that remained are holy, places families still go to bathe and pray. That's an old Hindu instinct: the earth itself is sacred. The Earth is honored as a goddess, Bhudevi, Mother Earth, and many Hindus, on waking, touch the floor before they step on it and say a short Sanskrit verse asking her to forgive them for touching her with their feet. Before a house is built, families hold a bhoomi puja, a worship of the ground, before the digging starts. So a story about one valley says out loud what every Hindu morning says quietly: the ground under you is holy. This week, more from the valley, starting from the lake.
screen: `THE LAKE OF SATI` · `KASHYAPA ASKS, THE LAKE DRAINS` · `A HOLY VALLEY` · `THE EARTH IS A GODDESS`

segments.voice: Before you get up from where you're sitting, lower one hand and touch the floor, the way many Hindus do on waking, then bring that hand to your forehead or your heart. Let it be a small sorry and thank you to the ground that holds you all day. If you know the morning verse to Mother Earth, say it; if you don't pray, let the touch itself be your thanks.
Kashmir. The valley that, the Nilamata Purana says, was once the lake of Sati, drained when the sage Kashyapa asked the gods for help. Today's word.
Hold on to this: the earth is holy; we ask her pardon. A valley began, the story says, as a goddess's lake. Until tomorrow.
